profiles.meeting_scenario: The meeting is a planning session at a tertiary academic cancer center to set up a 3-month pilot workflow for using quantitative imaging biomarkers in neuro-oncology. The pilot will support the weekly Wednesday brain tumor board for adults with suspected diffuse glioma by adding physiological MRI metrics and, when available, amino-acid PET summaries to routine structural imaging. The agenda is to decide which patients enter the pilot, what scan will count as the baseline timepoint, what deliverable will be available for tumor board, how quality control will be handled, and who owns each step before the pilot starts next month. The expected outcome is a practical workflow with roles, timeline, and a shared-looking plan for launching the pilot on the first Wednesday of the next scheduling block.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.role: Neuroradiologist and Director of Quantitative Neuroimaging
members.expertise: Physiological MRI, amino-acid PET interpretation, image post-processing, biomarker standardization
members.background: Lena trained in neuroradiology and completed a fellowship in advanced neuroimaging; she now runs the imaging core that supports neuro-oncology studies and has been trying to make DSC perfusion, diffusion, and PET-derived metrics reproducible enough for clinical research use.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to produce technically clean, defensible biomarker data without overloading her small post-processing team, and she is especially concerned that heterogeneous outside scans and rushed review will create noisy outputs that later get treated as if they were validated.
hidden_assumptions: For quantitative work, the baseline scan should be the last in-house preoperative or pre-biopsy scan acquired on the center's harmonized protocol, because that is the only point she considers technically comparable across patients.

When people say the pilot will cover newly diagnosed glioma cases, they mean patients whose imaging was performed at the center with the required MRI sequences; outside studies may help clinically but are not part of the quantitative cohort.

A board-ready deliverable can be a concise internal slide or screenshot with provisional maps and metrics discussed verbally at tumor board, even if no finalized radiology report has been signed in the electronic record.

Quality control means checking for gross motion, obvious susceptibility contamination, leakage-correction failure, and whether the lesion can be segmented; it does not require sequence-by-sequence harmonization or reprocessing every borderline case before discussion.

members.name: Dr. Miguel Alvarez
members.role: Neuro-oncologist and Clinical Lead for the Adult Glioma Program
members.expertise: Adult diffuse glioma management, trial enrollment, multidisciplinary treatment planning, longitudinal outcomes registries
members.background: Miguel is a medical neuro-oncologist who chairs parts of the weekly brain tumor board and oversees a prospective registry for newly diagnosed diffuse glioma; he is focused on making advanced imaging useful at the point of treatment decisions and easy to integrate with coordinator workflows.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to capture enough real-world patients to be clinically meaningful and to fit existing coordinator processes, and he worries that narrow eligibility or informal outputs will make surgeons and radiation oncologists ignore the biomarker work.
hidden_assumptions: Baseline should mean the first scan after pathology confirms diffuse glioma and before any oncologic treatment starts, because that is the registry time zero and the clinically meaningful comparison point.

When people say newly diagnosed adult glioma cases, they mean all adults presented at the tumor board for initial treatment planning, including referred patients whose outside MRI or PET is still the imaging basis for decisions.
A board-ready summary should be documented in the electronic health record or official tumor board note so downstream clinicians can act on it without relying on an internal slide deck.

Quality control means the derived maps and numbers are reliable enough for cross-patient and follow-up comparison, which usually implies sequence compliance, reprocessing when needed, and exclusion of nonstandard acquisitions rather than just a visual sanity check.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the baseline scan
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to capture biomarkers on the patient's baseline scan.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the last in-house scan before surgery or biopsy, because it is the standardized preoperative acquisition she trusts for quantitative extraction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the first post-pathology, pre-treatment scan, because that is how his registry defines baseline for outcomes and treatment planning.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Baseline is a routine clinical-research term that both use fluently, and in many patients the preoperative and pre-treatment scans are close enough in time that the mismatch feels inconsequential during planning.

misalignment_points.topic: Which patients are in the pilot cohort
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the pilot should cover newly diagnosed adult glioma cases coming to Wednesday tumor board.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes only patients with center-acquired harmonized MRI, with outside scans serving only as clinical reference until an in-house protocol is obtained.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes essentially all adults discussed for initial management, including referred patients whose outside MRI or PET is the basis for that week's decisions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds operationally complete because both are thinking about the same clinic population and the same board, while the inclusion boundary hides inside an unspoken assumption about scan provenance.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes the biomarker output board-ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the team needs a board-ready summary each Wednesday morning.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks board-ready means her team has a concise internal slide with provisional maps, lesion ROIs, and a few extracted metrics available for discussion at the meeting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks board-ready means the findings are entered into the formal tumor board note or radiology documentation in the EHR so they can be referenced afterward by surgery, radiation oncology, and coordinators.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They share the same practical goal of having information available before the conference, and neither sees a need to unpack whether 'ready' refers to discussion logistics or formal clinical documentation.

misalignment_points.topic: How much quality control is implied before sharing numbers
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that QC should happen before any quantitative numbers go out.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a neuroradiology fellow or analyst will do a rapid visual QC for obvious artifacts and then release preliminary metrics if the maps look usable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes QC includes checking protocol compliance, confirming comparability of derived values, and reprocessing or excluding borderline cases before those numbers reach the board or the registry.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: QC sounds like a universally shared safeguard, so both hear it as reassurance rather than as a place where workflow intensity and acceptable uncertainty might diverge.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this pilot narrow enough that my imaging core can actually execute it. If we stick to technically clean MRI perfusion, diffusion, and the occasional amino-acid PET where we have usable data, we can show value without generating a pile of noisy pseudo-quantitative numbers. The key is a manageable Wednesday workflow starting next month, with clear handoffs and no expectation that we rescue every messy study.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. If we can leave with a clear patient flow, who does what on Monday through Wednesday, and what the board will actually receive, we should be in good shape to launch on the first week of the next scheduling block.

turns.inner_thought: The pilot only matters if it reflects real clinical volume. I want essentially every newly diagnosed adult diffuse glioma patient who comes to Wednesday board for initial planning included, not just the subset with ideal internal imaging. Otherwise the surgeons and radiation oncologists will see it as a boutique side project. If we start with that population, the imaging can shape treatment decisions from the outset.
